reviewer.origin: Claude Agent tool subagent, model sonnet, a fresh context with only this brief and its files, launched 2026-10-26 by session_01Mxpoi6tFT3FgKmBvtGjRtS (the writer's session)

evidence: Draft: "You may have fooled yourself in the past and this part knows it. Try “Tell me what you remember, I'm listening.”" for his own words from the inner child guide: "Maybe you've fooled yourself before, and that part remembers. “Tell me what you remember, I'm listening.” works well here." It does what the_change says (Emulate's two sentences for his two, capital T like the paragraph's other scripts), and CONTEXT.txt holds it once, closing the second paragraph of the 'It feels fake' section after his unchanged "If it says yes, that one can sting, because there could be something to it." Meaning: kept are the point that the reader may have fooled themselves before, the part's awareness of it, and his script line word for word. Two small shifts that I judge fair but that the author should see: 'that part remembers' became 'this part knows it' (the echo with 'what you remember' is looser, though the next sentence still follows), and 'works well here' became 'Try', so his endorsement of the line becomes a plain suggestion of it. The advice to the reader is the same and nothing is added (no new claim, fact or first-person detail); his words show first on the card, so he can keep the endorsement. Seam and voice: the draft sentence explains the sting in the sentence before it, so the setup is visible (T03 absent); 'may have' sits with the section's own hedges ('could be', 'could say', 'might be'); 'this part' is the protecting part of the first paragraph and the 'it' that says yes, and the 'it' in 'knows it' is that you fooled yourself, so C02 is fine; I found no summary, reassurance or hedge he would not write. The double-quoted script among single-quoted lines is already in the words it replaces, so the change does not create that. Tell rows: I went through T01-T29 and C01-C04 on the literal draft in its context and found none PRESENT. Closest calls, judged absent: T02/T20/T22 (the paragraph now ends on a short instruction plus a quoted line, and each of the four paragraphs of the section ends on an instruction): that cadence is his own in paragraphs one, three and four, this paragraph carries stance and reason ('that one can sting', 'something to it', the part knowing), and the quote is the thing the reader is told to say, not a flourish; T29: the last sentence is a new step, not a restatement; T15 (same shape reworded: Maybe you've / before / that part remembers to You may have / in the past / this part knows it): the words are common ones, with no rare or odd swaps, so it is a plain rewording and not a thesaurus effect; T13: one echo is lost (remembers / remember) but the passage still notices things. Every other row is absent: no first-person stake, scene, prop, filler, contrast, colon, tic word, naming or fact claim. Linter: 'B7 short landing at paragraph end' accepted: the last sentence is the step the paragraph has been leading to (a line to say to the part), not a summing-up, and it is the section's only quoted ending, not one of a run; it does land a little more sharply than the old paragraph, which ran on into 'works well here' after the quote, which is the shift noted above. 'D9 follows the source order' accepted: two sentences for two, in the order the sense needs (the part knows, then ask what it remembers), and both still notice something. 'E36/E41 heavy second person' (9.5 per 100) accepted: 2 'you' in 21 words, the same two in the 19 words it replaces, the sentences before it in the paragraph run about 8.7 per 100, and the second 'you' addresses the part inside the script, not the reader.
